tldr: When a robot opens doors or drawers, this physical environment mapping method instantly shares estimated physical parameters from a single measured pull to look-alike furniture, deciding whether an action can safely succeed within a stated risk in milliseconds.
hero_caption: Overview of PhysVLMM. Across look-alike drawers in the same room (blue), measuring a single real pull (orange) updates the physical parameter priors of untouched drawers in closed form via Bayesian inference.
overview:
For mobile manipulators to open and close furniture, they need to predict not just which way a door swings, but its physical response: how much force is needed to keep it moving, and whether it will hit an obstacle along the way. Conventional scene maps and Vision-Language-Motion Maps (VLMMs) only record what objects are and whether they have moved, without predicting their responses to applied forces. On the other hand, methods like differentiable simulation can identify physical dynamics, but they require repeated probing of each object and suffer from heavy computational costs.

This work leverages the fact that human environments naturally contain rows of identical, co-installed furniture. Dynamically, visual observation alone cannot identify dynamic parameters, and pulling in a single direction introduces an unidentifiable direction where Coulomb friction and preload cannot be separated. The authors address this with "PhysVLMM," which retains the unidentifiable direction as a posterior distribution rather than a point estimate, and immediately shares force evidence from one pull to untouched look-alike furniture using closed-form updates.

Evaluated on a dataset of 18 real homes and simulated environments, PhysVLMM cuts prediction error by 41 % compared to differentiable simulation while running roughly four orders of magnitude faster (13 ms vs. 230 s). It also demonstrates safe query decisions that stay within user-specified risk limits.
contributions: Theoretically showed that dynamics parameters cannot be identified from visual observation without force measurements, and that single-direction pulls leave an unidentifiable direction in parameter space.

Constructed a physical map update algorithm that retains the unidentifiable parameter direction as a posterior distribution and immediately propagates evidence to untouched look-alike parts in closed form.
Developed a query mechanism that answers planner queries like "can this safely be pulled with this force?" with "Yes, No, or Abstain" within a specified risk threshold at 0.03 ms per query.

sections.heading: Why robots need to know how "heavy" furniture is before pulling
sections.summary: To open doors and drawers, robots must predict physical responses to their actions, not just kinematic articulation. Because uninstrumented observation or single pulls cannot fully identify dynamics, this paper proposes sharing evidence across look-alike furniture in a scene map.
sections.details:
For mobile robots performing tidying or delivery tasks, the first step is often opening cabinets or refrigerators. The robot must know more than just "can it move?" or "which way does it swing?" It must determine whether it can sustain motion with its available pull force and whether the door will collide with nearby obstacles. Misjudging this can stall motors or damage the environment.

Prior work has explored joint estimation and scene graphs that infer mass or materials from images. However, existing scene maps do not predict responses to concrete actions. While recent methods use differentiable simulation to identify dynamics, they require individual probing for every object and do not transfer knowledge to untouched furniture.

A fundamental roadblock here is the limit of parameter identifiability. Watching motion without force sensors cannot identify dynamics, as any combination of friction, damping, and inertia can reproduce the observed trajectory (Proposition 1). Furthermore, even when measuring pull forces, a single-direction pull cannot separate Coulomb friction from preload springs (Proposition 2). Therefore, identifying untouched parts must rely on transferring evidence from other parts already pulled in the same building.

PhysVLMM extends existing Vision-Language-Motion Maps (VLMMs) by attaching physical beliefs to each articulated part. By sharing force evidence across look-alike furniture in the building, the robot can anticipate the required effort before ever touching the object.

sections.heading: Pull once, inform the rest: closed-form belief updates and risk-bounded queries
sections.summary: Grounded in equations of motion and identifiability theory, PhysVLMM retains single-pull uncertainty as a posterior distribution. Hierarchical Bayesian sharing among look-alike groups updates the required effort for untouched parts and swiftly checks safety within a stated risk.
sections.details:
### 2.1 Problem formulation and representation
Each element in the scene map is augmented with joint geometry $\mathcal{G}_i$ (axes and limits), a mechanism and parameter belief $\mathcal{B}_{i,t}$, and a response distribution $\mathcal{R}_{i,t}$ for queried actions. Part motion is modeled by a 5D parameter vector $\theta_i=(I,b,\tau_c,k,\tau_0)$ consisting of inertia $I$, viscous damping $b$, Coulomb friction $\tau_c$, spring stiffness $k$, and preload $\tau_0$. The steady-state pull force needed to move the part at constant speed is defined as effort $x_i = \log \bar{F}_i$.

### 2.2 Identifiability and core design
Theoretical analysis proves that $\theta$ is completely unidentifiable from unforced motion observation alone (Proposition 1). Moreover, even with force measurements during a single-direction pull, the regressor matrix is rank-deficient, identifying only the sum of Coulomb friction and preload (Proposition 2). Forcing a point estimate produces severe bias. PhysVLMM instead preserves the unidentifiable spread directly in the posterior covariance.

### 2.3 Algorithmic workflow
- **Geometry and joint inference (M3)**: Trajectories are fitted with pure translation (prismatic) and rigid rotation (revolute), identifying axes and joint types using BIC and logistic regression.
- **Posterior for the pulled part (M4)**: A regressor matrix from the pull updates a Gaussian covariance, keeping the prior variance along the unidentifiable direction.
- **Sharing across look-alikes (M4)**: Parts sharing visual appearance and orientation form "look-alike groups." Using a hierarchical normal model for effort within each group, evidence from one pull updates the predictive distribution of untouched parts in closed form with just two additions.
- **Risk-conditioned queries (M5, M6)**: When a planner asks if a force $F$ can safely open a part, PhysVLMM computes the success probability. Given an allowed risk $\delta$, it returns "Yes" if success $\ge 1-\delta$, "No" if failure $\ge 1-\delta$, and otherwise "Abstain" due to insufficient evidence.

sections.heading: Tested in 18 real homes: four orders of magnitude faster than simulation with higher accuracy
sections.summary: Evaluated across 18 real homes (Hoi! dataset) and 120 simulated kitchens, PhysVLMM cuts prediction error by 41 % over differentiable simulation (RigPI) while dropping computation time from 230 seconds to 13 milliseconds, keeping risk-conditioned queries provably safe.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Experimental setup
Real-world evaluations used the Hoi! dataset, where humans opened and closed furniture in 18 homes with a force-sensing gripper. Simulation experiments used 120 RoboCasa kitchen environments where a robot pulled furniture with constant forces (3 to 12 N).

### 3.2 Comparison with baselines
- **Joint-type identification**: While single-view methods like FlowBot3D (48 %) and GAPartNet (39 %) struggled, PhysVLMM leveraged observed link motion to reach 86 % accuracy (88.6 % over all 306 pulls).
- **Response prediction**: In predicting responses to held-out pulls from estimated parameters, RigPI (differentiable simulation) achieved a CRPS of 0.544, while PhysVLMM achieved 0.323, reducing error by 41 %.
- **Compute speed**: RigPI required a median of 230 seconds per case. PhysVLMM completed in just 13 ms on a single CPU thread—over four orders of magnitude faster. Query evaluations alone took only 0.03 ms.

### 3.3 Ablations and risk control
- **Force prediction on untouched parts**: Keeping individual priors yielded a typical error of 56 %, which dropped to 42 % once evidence was shared across look-alikes.
- **Risk-calibrated decisions**: Across risk tolerances $\delta$ from 0.02 to 0.30, the false-safe rate (answering "Yes" when the force actually stalled) stayed strictly within $\delta$.
- **Look-alike groups vs. home-wide pooling**: Pooling all identical-type furniture across an entire home performed nearly as well as fine-grained look-alike groups. Because humans pulled parts all the way open in the real data, a simple baseline predicting motion to the mechanical stop was also strong for final position. However, in simulation with constant-force pulls that could stall, the full physical belief model proved superior.

sections.heading: Conclusions and future directions
sections.summary: PhysVLMM couples posterior tracking with closed-form evidence sharing to address fundamental identifiability limits. It decisively outperforms differentiable simulation in speed and accuracy, paving the way for integration with full perception pipelines and broader mechanism classes.
sections.details:
This paper introduced PhysVLMM, incorporating physical beliefs of articulated objects into robot scene maps. Based on two dynamical propositions—that passive vision cannot identify dynamic parameters, and single-direction pulls leave an unidentifiable manifold—the system adopts three core designs: (1) preserving the unidentifiable direction as a posterior distribution, (2) sharing evidence with untouched look-alike parts via closed-form updates, and (3) answering queries at a declared risk threshold.

Evaluations across 18 real homes showed that PhysVLMM achieves both superior speed and accuracy over existing methods, delivering query response times suitable for safe online motion planning.

Future work includes extending the formulation to other mechanisms such as trash can lids, windows, and valves, running real-robot experiments with constant-force pulls and collisions, and integrating with fully autonomous, annotation-free perception pipelines.

sections.heading: Appendix: identifiability proofs and collision checking
sections.summary: This section provides mathematical proofs for the identifiability propositions, discusses unit-testing fixes using manufactured solutions, and evaluates point-cloud sweep collision checking.
sections.details:
- **Proofs of propositions**: When external forces $\tau_{\mathrm{ext}}$ can be arbitrarily chosen, any parameter vector $\theta$ can satisfy the equations of motion for some trajectory, making dynamics unidentifiable (Proposition 1). When pulling in a single direction, columns of the regressor matrix become linearly dependent, making Coulomb friction and preload inseparable (Proposition 2).
- **Manufactured solutions**: Unit tests using synthetic data with known ground truth uncovered three critical bugs during development, including one where end-stop collision samples contaminated data and distorted inertia estimates.
- **Collision checking challenges**: Evaluating collisions via point-cloud sweeps yielded a 23 % false-positive rate on real data, mistakenly tagging furniture handles or adjacent cabinetry as obstacles. In simulation, it missed 59 % of collisions (false negatives), indicating that the collision module still requires improvement to provide reliable safety guarantees.

takeaways: Visual observation without force data provably cannot identify dynamic parameters, and single-direction pulls cannot separate Coulomb friction from preload; maintaining uncertainties as a posterior rather than a point estimate is essential.
Leveraging the prior that homes contain identical furniture, a hierarchical Bayesian model transfers force observations in closed form (just two additions) to untouched parts.
Analytically reasoning over 1-DOF joint dynamics replaces heavy online differentiable simulation, predicting responses four orders of magnitude faster (in milliseconds) with greater robustness.
limitations: Point-cloud sweep collision checking remains imprecise, frequently misclassifying handles as obstacles or missing real collisions in simulation, falling short of providing safety guarantees.
Real-world evaluations relied on oracle annotations for object identification and 3D bounding boxes; robustness against noisy outputs from fully autonomous perception pipelines remains unverified.
The real dataset (Hoi!) predominantly consists of human pulls that move parts all the way to their stops; constant-force pulls that stall mid-trajectory were only evaluated in simulation.
